card_quote: What counts as useful to him: a fact he can turn into a quiz question or win an argument with; sources matter when the quizmaster is challenged. / Narrative: Team captain for a decade; keeps a notebook of questions that caught his team out.
how_read: Cover to cover, a round a night or so, notebook open. I read the question, made my call, then mostly read the verdict, the first paragraph and the Tell someone line, and only went through the full answer when it was one I'd got wrong or might get challenged on. Took me about a week of evenings and a couple of goes in the pub before the quiz.

w1_friction.note: Went to the contents to jump to round five and it sent me two pages short, into the end of round four. Page numbers are off from there on.
Murphy's law comes out 'disputed'. Fine for a book, useless for a quiz. You can't mark a table on 'not settled'.
w1_friction.quote: Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled.

w1_friction.note: The 65 percent is right for the main condition, by the book's own first line. Any quizmaster would accept TRUE there. Calling it DISPUTED is moving the goalposts.
w1_friction.quote: About 65 percent of participants went to the maximum 450 volts

w1_friction.note: A Franklin kite question in the middle of round four with the wrong round header and a second number 31. Looks like a page got in from somewhere else.
Verdict says TRUE and the very next line says it's an embellishment. Then the Tell someone line says he never did it. Which is it? I'd get lynched reading that out.
w1_friction.quote: Franklin never flew a kite in a thunderstorm

w1_friction.note: One Wikipedia link as the only source, when every other page lists three or four. Wouldn't stand up to a challenge.
American spellings throughout, armor, color, behavior. Not a big deal but it reads like a US book.
w1_friction.quote: Did Wald really tell the military to armor

w1_friction.note: Second Wald plane in a row. Lots of these pairs: two apples, two Hanlons, two Dunning-Krugers, two Laffers. Half the time question two gives away question one.
w1_friction.quote: The record treats the anecdote as partly embellished

w1_friction.note: Eskimo snow words, another 'depends what you count'. I'd have taken FOLKLORE as the pub answer; the book wriggles.
w1_friction.quote: The answer depends on what counts as a word.

w1_friction.note: Goldfish memory in round eight, headed 'Names that mislead', and numbered 71 again. Same problem as the Franklin page.
Reads like a lab report somebody fed through a thesaurus. Couldn't read this aloud to anyone. And 'various laboratory studies' isn't a source.
Odd line. If you've got nothing more on the trumpeters, just don't say it.
w1_friction.quote: The record gives no further detail of the experiment

w1_friction.note: The page numbers on the surprises list don't match. Toast says p. 188 and the answer's a few pages later. Also 'fooled the most people' according to who?
w1_friction.quote: The stories that fooled the most people, ranked.

w1_best.why: Blood, toil, tears and sweat. Classic, and the Hansard date makes it challenge-proof.
Crud not crap. Great tiebreaker question, short and certain.
Hanoi rat tails. Lovely story and the book shows the cobra one is the dodgy version. Two questions in one for a quiz.
Hooke's anagram. Nobody will know it and it's dead certain.
Streisand photo downloaded six times, two of them by her lawyers. That's a cracker of a fact.

w1_flat.why: Thucydides trap. More a politics seminar than a quiz question, and it ends 'disputed'.
Uncertainty principle. Too abstract to make a question out of.
The goldfish one in round eight. Unreadable, and it's in the wrong place.
Overton window naming. Nobody at my table has heard of Overton.
Milgram 65 percent. The verdict's a fudge.

w1_review.headline: Good quiz fodder, but check it before you use it
w1_review.body: Plenty here I'll lift for our pub quiz, and I like that every answer names its sources, which is what you need when someone challenges you. I knew maybe a third of it already from QI, and the answers are far too long to read out; the Tell someone line is the bit that's actually usable. There are some careless bits that worry me: a Franklin page that says TRUE and then says the opposite, a goldfish page in the wrong round, and contents and index page numbers that don't line up. Bottom line: three stars, good source material for a quizmaster, but sort out the mistakes.

w2_review_first: If you run or play a pub quiz, there's a good thirty or forty questions in it with sources to back them up. Read the bold line at the end of each answer and skip the rest. A couple of pages look like they got in by accident, so don't trust it blind.

w2_lost.why: The Franklin page put me off for a night. If one verdict is printed backwards, how many others are?
Round seven got into nuclear strategy and the Thucydides stuff, and I left it till the next evening.
The goldfish page, gave up halfway through the first sentence.

w2_read_aloud.why: Sturgeon's 'crud'. Short, funny, and you can mark it.
Churchill's four words. Everyone gets it wrong.
Rat tails in Hanoi. Gets a laugh and a groan.
Muphry's law spelled wrong on purpose. Good one for the editors in the room.
Trumpeters on a train. Sounds made up, it isn't. Perfect quiz trap.

w2_cut.title: Do goldfish have a three-second memory?
w2_cut.why: Unreadable, misnumbered and sourced to nothing.

w2_cut.title: Did Benjamin Franklin fly a kite in a thunderstorm?
w2_cut.why: Verdict contradicts its own answer. Cut it or fix it.
Ends in an argument about method, not an answer.
No one can play it without a physics degree.
Repeats the apple question right before it and gives the game away.

w2_book2: More pages with the verdict contradicting the answer, or more 'disputed' answers I can't use in a quiz.
